part7: Part Seven: The Last Week in Jerusalem
ch42.title: Entering Jerusalem
ch42.b002: The day after the memorable sermon on “The Kingdom of Heaven,” Jesus announced that he and the apostles would go up to Jerusalem for the Passover, visiting many cities of southern Perea on the way. To nearly all his followers the news could mean only one thing: the Master was going up at last to set up the kingdom in Jerusalem. No matter what Jesus said about its spiritual nature, he could not wholly remove that hope from their minds.
ch42.b003: That Sunday afternoon Salome, the mother of James and John Zebedee, came to Jesus with her two apostle sons. In the manner of one approaching an Oriental potentate, she wanted him to promise in advance to grant whatever she might ask. The Master would not promise. Instead he asked her, “⟦Q 171:0.4⟧What do you want me to do for you?⟦/Q⟧” She asked that her sons might sit, the one on his right hand and the other on his left, in his kingdom. Jesus said, “⟦Q 171:0.5⟧Woman, you know not what you ask.⟦/Q⟧” Then, looking straight into the eyes of the two honor-seeking apostles, he asked them, “⟦Q 171:0.5⟧Are you able to drink the cup I am about to drink?⟦/Q⟧” Without a moment for thought they answered, “Yes, Master, we are able.” He was grieved that they did not understand the nature of his kingdom; yet he knew they loved him, and he declared that they would indeed drink of his cup of bitterness and share in his humiliation. But to sit on his right hand and on his left was not his to give; such honors were reserved for those designated by his Father.
ch42.b004: Word of the conference soon reached Peter and the others, and they were highly indignant. When they fell to arguing among themselves, Jesus called them all together. “⟦Q 171:0.6⟧Whosoever would be great among you, let him first become your servant. He who would be first in the kingdom, let him become your minister. I declare to you that the Son of Man came not to be ministered to but to minister; and I now go up to Jerusalem to lay down my life in the doing of the Father’s will and in the service of my brethren.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles withdrew by themselves to pray, and that evening, through the labors of Peter, James and John made suitable apologies to the ten. None of them dreamed that in less than a month their beloved teacher would hang on a Roman cross, with a dying thief on one side and another transgressor on the other. Their mother would be standing there, and she would remember her foolish request.
ch42.b006: On the forenoon of Monday, March 13, Jesus and the twelve took final leave of the Pella encampment. About a thousand disciples followed after them. At the Bethany ford of the Jordan, when the crowd realized he was not going straight to Jerusalem and began to argue, Jesus climbed upon a huge stone and spoke to them. Whoever would follow him from that time on, he said, must be willing to pay the price of wholehearted dedication to the Father’s will, even to the giving up of life itself. Who would build a watchtower without first sitting down to count the cost? What king would go to war against twenty thousand with ten thousand without first taking counsel? “⟦Q 171:2.5⟧Now have I warned you to turn back to your homes in peace if you are not willing to drink with me the cup which is being prepared. Again and again have I told you that my kingdom is not of this world, but you will not believe me. He who has ears to hear let him hear what I say.⟦/Q⟧”
ch42.b007: When he had finished, he set off with the twelve on the road to Heshbon, and about five hundred went with him. After a brief delay the other half of the multitude went on up to Jerusalem. For more than two weeks the little company journeyed through the towns of southern Perea where the seventy were at work. At Heshbon Jesus met Abner. It was the last time Abner ever saw him in the flesh. His farewell was simple: “⟦Q 171:3.2⟧My son, I know you will be true to the kingdom, and I pray the Father to grant you wisdom that you may love and understand your brethren.⟦/Q⟧” From town to town the followers dwindled, as many hurried on to the feast, until fewer than two hundred walked with him day by day.
ch42.b009: The apostles knew that the Sanhedrin had proclaimed to all Israel that Jesus had been condemned to die. Yet they were not so afraid as before, for they had seen Lazarus come out of the tomb. Surely, they thought, in an emergency the Master would assert his divine power and put his enemies to shame. On Wednesday evening, March 29, the company camped at Livias, and that night Simon Zelotes and Simon Peter, who had arranged to have more than one hundred swords delivered there, handed them out to all who would accept them. The men wore them hidden beneath their cloaks.
ch42.b010: Early on Thursday morning, before the others were awake, Jesus called Andrew and said, “⟦Q 171:4.2⟧Awaken your brethren! I have something to say to them.⟦/Q⟧” He knew about the swords and which of his apostles were wearing them, but he never disclosed that he knew. He warned them not to trust in the frailties of man’s defense, and once more told them plainly that the Son of Man would be delivered to the chief priests and then to the gentiles, to be mocked, scourged, and put to death. “⟦Q 171:4.2⟧And when they kill the Son of Man, be not dismayed, for I declare that on the third day he shall rise. Take heed to yourselves and remember that I have forewarned you.⟦/Q⟧” They were stunned, yet they could not bring themselves to take his words literally. The “third day” was a common Jewish expression meaning “soon,” and when he spoke of “rising,” they thought he meant the rising of the kingdom.
ch42.b011: Just after breakfast certain friendly Pharisees came with a warning: Herod, who had killed John, now sought to kill him too, and he had better flee. Jesus knew Herod better than they did. The tetrarch feared him and would far rather see him die in Jerusalem at the hands of the chief priests than stain his own hands again. “⟦Q 171:4.6⟧Go you and tell that fox that the Son of Man preaches in Perea today, tomorrow goes into Judea, and after a few days, will be perfected in his mission on earth and prepared to ascend to the Father.⟦/Q⟧” Then he turned to his apostles, and his voice was full of sorrow: “⟦Q 171:4.7⟧O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones the teachers of truth! How often would I have gathered your children together even as a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, but you would not let me do it!⟦/Q⟧”
ch42.b013: Late on Thursday afternoon, March 30, Jesus and his apostles, at the head of some two hundred followers, approached the walls of Jericho. Near the gate sat a crowd of beggars, among them Bartimeus, an elderly man blind from his youth. Hearing the heavy tramp of the multitude, he asked what was happening, and one of the beggars told him, “⟦Q 171:5.2⟧Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.⟦/Q⟧” At once he lifted up his voice: “⟦Q 171:5.2⟧Jesus, Jesus, have mercy upon me!⟦/Q⟧” Those near Jesus rebuked him, but he only cried the louder. Jesus stood still and said, “Bring the man to me.” Bartimeus threw aside his cloak and sprang toward the middle of the road. “⟦Q 171:0.4⟧What do you want me to do for you?⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 171:5.3⟧I would have my sight restored.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 171:5.3⟧You shall receive your sight; go your way; your faith has made you whole.⟦/Q⟧” Immediately he could see, and he stayed near Jesus, glorifying God.
ch42.b014: The sun was going down when the procession passed the customs house. Zaccheus, the rich chief publican, wanted to see Jesus, but he was short of stature and could not see over the crowd. So he ran on ahead and climbed into a sycamore tree whose branches overhung the road. When Jesus came to the tree, he stopped and looked up. “⟦Q 171:6.1⟧Make haste, Zaccheus, and come down, for tonight I must abide at your house.⟦/Q⟧” Zaccheus nearly fell out of the tree in his haste. At his door a Pharisee standing near by sneered that this man had gone to lodge with a sinner, an extortioner and a robber of his own people. Jesus looked down at Zaccheus and smiled. Then Zaccheus stood upon a stool and declared to the men of Jericho that he would give half of all his goods to the poor and, if he had wrongfully taken anything from any man, would restore it fourfold. Jesus said: “⟦Q 171:6.3⟧Today has salvation come to this home, and you have become indeed a son of Abraham.⟦/Q⟧” And to the crowd he added, “⟦Q 171:6.3⟧I have all along declared that the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which is lost.⟦/Q⟧”
ch42.b015: That was how Jesus always worked. Most of the really important things he said or did seemed to happen casually, “as he passed by.” He was never in a hurry, and he was always ready to stop a sermon while he ministered to a single person, even a little child.
ch42.b016: It was nearly noon the next day before they set out up the “road of robbers” toward Bethany. Halfway up they stopped for lunch, and there Jesus told the apostles the parable of the pounds, of a nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom, entrusted a pound to each of his servants, and on his return called them to account. “⟦Q 171:8.3⟧You think that the Son of Man goes up to Jerusalem to receive a kingdom,⟦/Q⟧” he said, “⟦Q 171:8.3⟧but I declare that you are doomed to disappointment.⟦/Q⟧” When they had eaten, he stood before them in the shade of an overhanging rock and, with cheerful dignity, pointed westward. “⟦Q 171:8.14⟧Come, my brethren, let us go on into Jerusalem, there to receive that which awaits us; thus shall we fulfill the will of the heavenly Father in all things.⟦/Q⟧”
ch42.b018: Shortly after four o’clock on Friday afternoon, March 31, they arrived at Bethany. So many people were coming every day to talk with Lazarus about his resurrection that Jesus stayed with a neighboring believer, Simon, the leading citizen of the village. Jesus was majestically calm; his friends had never seen him more composed and congenial. That night, while the Master slept, the apostles watched over him by twos, and many of them were girded with swords.
ch42.b019: On the evening after the Sabbath, six days before the Passover, all Bethany and Bethpage gathered at Simon’s house for a public banquet in honor of Jesus and Lazarus, given in open defiance of the Sanhedrin. Martha directed the serving; her sister Mary stood among the women onlookers, for it was against Jewish custom for a woman to sit at a public banquet. Near the close of the feast Mary stepped forward, went to where Jesus reclined, and opened a large alabaster cruse of very rare and costly ointment. She anointed his head, then poured it upon his feet, took down her hair, and wiped them with it. The whole house was filled with the fragrance. Some murmured at the waste, and Judas Iscariot went over to Andrew and asked why the ointment had not been sold and the money given to feed the poor.
ch42.b020: Jesus put his hand upon Mary’s head as she knelt by his side. “⟦Q 172:1.6⟧Let her alone, every one of you. Why do you trouble her about this, seeing that she has done a good thing in her heart? … you have the poor always with you so that you may minister to them at any time it seems good to you; but I shall not always be with you; I go soon to my Father.⟦/Q⟧” Mary, he said, had long saved this ointment for his burial, and by anointing him now she showed that she believed what he had told them about his death. The ointment had cost as much as one man earned in a year, enough to buy bread for five thousand people. Judas took the rebuke as a personal reproof, and that night, for the first time, he dared to think of revenge in his open and conscious mind.
ch42.b022: On Sunday, April 2, Jesus resolved to enter the city openly. Until now he had suppressed all public acclaim of himself as the Messiah, but his death had been decreed, and the end was near. He well knew how this visit would end. Of all the prophecies he chose one: “⟦Q 172:3.4⟧Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you. He is just and he brings salvation. He comes as the lowly one, riding upon an ass, upon a colt, the foal of an ass.⟦/Q⟧” A warrior king entered a city on a horse; a king on a mission of peace rode a donkey. What he had failed to teach in words, he would now try to show in a sign. He sent Peter and John to Bethpage, where they found a colt tied near its mother. When the owner asked what they were doing, he said, “⟦Q 172:3.6⟧If your Master is Jesus from Galilee, let him have the colt.⟦/Q⟧”
ch42.b023: At half past one in the afternoon the Alpheus twins put their cloaks on the donkey and held him while the Master got on. As the procession climbed toward the summit of Olivet, the festive crowd threw their garments on the road and brought branches from the trees to make a carpet of honor, and they shouted together, “⟦Q 172:3.9⟧Hosanna to the son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus was lighthearted and cheerful until they reached the brow of the hill, where the city and the temple towers came into full view. There he stopped the procession, and a great silence fell upon them all as they saw him weeping. “⟦Q 172:3.10⟧O Jerusalem, if you had only known, even you, at least in this your day, the things which belong to your peace, and which you could so freely have had! … You are about to reject the gift of God, and all men will reject you.⟦/Q⟧”
ch42.b024: As they came down the slope, thousands of pilgrims, roused by the report David Zebedee had spread, poured out of the city waving palm branches and shouting hosannas. Some Pharisees pushed their way up beside him and told him to rebuke his disciples. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 172:3.13⟧It is only fitting that these children should welcome the Son of Peace, whom the chief priests have rejected. It would be useless to stop them lest in their stead these stones by the roadside cry out.⟦/Q⟧” The whole city was stirred, and everyone asked, “Who is this man?” Yet there was no deep conviction behind the cheering. These same crowds would turn away from him before the week was out.
ch42.b026: At the temple Jesus did not say a word to the crowds. He strolled with the ten through the courts, and no one dared lay a hand on him, for the Sanhedrin feared the people. As evening came on and the crowds went off to eat, they sat down for a moment by the treasury. A poor widow, scantily dressed, came by and cast two small coppers into the trumpet. “⟦Q 172:4.2⟧Heed well what you have just seen,⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said. “⟦Q 172:4.2⟧This poor widow cast in more than all the others, for all these others, from their superfluity, cast in some trifle as a gift, but this poor woman, even though she is in want, gave all that she had, even her living.⟦/Q⟧” Then he said, “⟦Q 172:4.3⟧Let us go up to Bethany for our rest.⟦/Q⟧” He walked ahead of them, and not a word was spoken all the way.
ch42.b027: No twelve men ever carried home such different feelings. Peter, who had longed to preach to that eager crowd, was inexpressibly saddened. Simon Zelotes, the noisiest man in the procession, had pictured the Sanhedrin dead before sunset; by five o’clock he was a silent, crushed, and disillusioned apostle. John remembered the words of Zechariah and grasped something of the meaning of the day. For the Alpheus twins it was the day they came nearest to heaven on earth. And there was Judas. Just as Jesus reached the city gate, a prominent Sadducee, a friend of his family, slapped him on the back and mocked him: let him cheer up and join them in hailing this Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews, as he rode through the gates on an ass. Judas had never shrunk from persecution, but he could not stand ridicule. He felt ashamed of his Master and his fellow apostles. At heart he was already a deserter; it only remained for him to find some plausible excuse for an open break.
ch43.title: Controversy in the Temple
ch43.b001: Monday Morning in the Temple Courts
ch43.b002: Early on Monday morning Jesus and the apostles gathered at Simon’s house in Bethany and, after a brief conference, set out for Jerusalem. As they went down the slope of Olivet, Jesus led the way and the twelve followed close behind in meditative silence. They had not yet recovered from the day before. In the minds of all save one there was a single question: What will the Master do today? The one absorbing thought of Judas Iscariot was different: What shall I do? Shall I go on with Jesus and my associates, or shall I withdraw? And if I am going to quit, how shall I break off?
ch43.b003: It was about nine o’clock on that beautiful morning when they reached the temple. The great courts had become a marketplace. Because the temple inspectors were quick to find a “blemish” in any animal a worshiper brought, most people bought their sacrifices from the temple pens, and the larger share of the profits went to the ruling high-priestly families. Licensed money-changers exchanged more than twenty sorts of foreign money for the Jewish silver required for the temple dues, taking a heavy commission. At one time the greedy priests had demanded a week’s wages for a pair of doves that should have been sold to the poor for a few pennies. The temple treasury might hold upwards of ten million dollars while the common people languished in poverty.
ch43.b004: Jesus mounted one of the teaching platforms, greeted the believers who were waiting for him, and began to speak, while the apostles withdrew a short distance. Then two things arrested his attention. At a nearby money table a violent argument had broken out over the overcharging of a Jew from Alexandria, and at the same moment the air was rent by the bellowing of some hundred bullocks being driven from one section of the pens to another. And close by he saw a simple-minded Galilean, a man he had once talked with in Iron, being ridiculed and jostled about by supercilious Judeans. All of this together stirred up in his soul one of those strange and periodic uprisings of indignant emotion.
ch43.b006: To the amazement of his apostles, Jesus stepped down from the platform, went over to the lad who was driving the cattle, took his whip of cords, and swiftly drove the animals out of the temple. Nor was that all. Before the wondering gaze of thousands, he strode majestically to the farthest cattle pen and opened the gates of every stall. By now the pilgrims were electrified. With uproarious shouting they surged toward the bazaars and began to overturn the tables of the money-changers. In less than five minutes all commerce had been swept from the temple. When the Roman guards appeared, all was quiet and the crowds were orderly. Jesus returned to the speaker’s stand and said: “⟦Q 173:1.7⟧You have this day witnessed that which is written in the Scriptures: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers.’⟦/Q⟧”
ch43.b007: Before he could say more, the great assembly broke out in hosannas, and a throng of youths stepped out to sing hymns of thanksgiving. When certain priests asked him whether he did not hear what the children of the Levites were saying, he answered, “⟦Q 173:1.8⟧Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings has praise been perfected’?⟦/Q⟧” All the rest of that day guards set by the people stood at every archway and would not let anyone carry even an empty vessel across the temple courts. It was a day of quiet and peace, and the people literally hung on his words. The apostles, taken completely by surprise, stayed huddled together near the speaker’s stand and never lifted a hand. The episode revealed the Master’s attitude toward the commercializing of religion and his detestation of every kind of unfairness and profiteering at the expense of the poor and the unlearned.
ch43.b009: When the chief priests and scribes heard what had happened, they were dumfounded. At the noon session of the Sanhedrin it was unanimously agreed that Jesus must be speedily destroyed, but they feared the multitude and could not agree on when and how to take him. Instead they appointed five groups to go among the people and try to entangle him in his teaching or discredit him in the eyes of his hearers. About two o’clock, just as Jesus had begun to speak on “The Liberty of Sonship,” a group of elders made their way up to him and asked: “⟦Q 173:2.2⟧By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?⟦/Q⟧”
ch43.b010: Jesus answered with a question of his own: “⟦Q 173:2.4⟧The baptism of John, whence was it? Did John get his authority from heaven or from men?⟦/Q⟧” They withdrew to one side to confer. If they said from heaven, he would ask why they had not believed John; if they said from men, the multitude, who held John to be a prophet, might turn on them. So they came back and said, “⟦Q 173:2.5⟧Concerning the baptism of John, we cannot answer; we do not know.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus looked down upon them and said, “⟦Q 173:2.5⟧Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.⟦/Q⟧” It was not an evasion. His authority was in himself and in his Father’s eternal supremacy, and even the common folk could see the difference between the Master’s moral majesty and the designing hypocrisy of his questioners.
ch43.b011: As the caviling Pharisees stood silent before him, Jesus told them a parable. A great landholder asked his two sons to work in his vineyard. One said, “I will not go,” but afterward repented and went. The other said, “⟦Q 173:3.1⟧Yes, my father, I will go,⟦/Q⟧” and did not go. “⟦Q 173:3.1⟧Let me ask you, which of these sons really did his father’s will?⟦/Q⟧” The people answered with one accord, “The first son.” Then Jesus declared that the publicans and harlots would go into the kingdom of God before those who made great pretensions of serving the Father but would not do his works. “⟦Q 173:3.2⟧It was not you, the Pharisees and scribes, who believed John, but rather the publicans and sinners; neither do you believe my teaching, but the common people hear my words gladly.⟦/Q⟧” He bore no personal hatred toward them; it was the inevitable clash between a new and living religion of the spirit and an older religion of ceremony, tradition, and authority.
ch43.b012: The Vineyard and the Wedding Feast
ch43.b013: Turning to the listening multitude, Jesus told another parable. A householder planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, built a watchtower, let it out to tenants, and went into another country. When the season of fruit came, he sent servants to collect his rent, but the tenants beat one, stoned another, and sent the rest away empty-handed. He sent more trusted servants, and even his steward, and they killed him. At last he sent his beloved son, thinking they would surely respect him. But the tenants said among themselves, “⟦Q 173:4.2⟧This is the heir; come, let us kill him and then the inheritance will be ours.⟦/Q⟧” So they cast him out of the vineyard and killed him. When some of the people perceived that the parable spoke of the nation and its treatment of the prophets, and of the rejection now at hand, they said in sorrow, “⟦Q 173:4.3⟧God forbid that we should go on doing these things.⟦/Q⟧”
ch43.b014: Seeing a group of Sadducees and Pharisees pushing through the crowd, Jesus waited until they drew near and then looked searchingly at them. “⟦Q 173:4.4⟧Did you never read in the Scripture about the stone which the builders rejected, and which, when the people had discovered it, was made into the cornerstone?⟦/Q⟧” If they continued to reject this gospel, he warned, the kingdom of God would be taken from them and given to a people who would bring forth the fruits of the spirit. The Pharisees knew he was speaking of them. They longed to lay hold on him then and there, but they feared the multitude. That night the Sadducees and the Pharisees joined hands in a plan to entrap him the next day.
ch43.b015: Then Jesus spoke the parable of the marriage feast. A king made a wedding feast for his son, but those who had been invited made light of the call and went their ways, “⟦Q 173:5.2⟧one to the farm, another to the pottery, and others to their merchandise,⟦/Q⟧” and some even seized and killed his messengers. So the king sent his servants into the highways and out-of-the-way places, and they gathered good and bad, rich and poor, until the wedding chamber was filled. Yet one guest came without the wedding garment the king had freely provided for all, and he was cast out. As Jesus was about to dismiss the crowd, a sympathetic believer asked what sign he would give that he was the Son of God. “⟦Q 173:5.4⟧Only one sign shall be given you.⟦/Q⟧” Then, pointing to his own body, he said, “⟦Q 173:5.4⟧Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.⟦/Q⟧” No one understood him, not even his apostles, until after his resurrection, when they remembered what he had said.
ch43.b016: About four o’clock Jesus beckoned to the apostles, and they left the temple for Bethany. On the way up Olivet he told Andrew, Philip, and Thomas to set up a camp nearer the city for the rest of the Passover week; the next morning they pitched their tents in a hillside ravine overlooking the public camping park of Gethsemane. Once again it was a silent group that climbed the slope that night. The morning had raised their hopes; the afternoon had pointed to his certain rejection. They felt that something tremendous was about to happen, though they did not know what. They slept very little. Even the Alpheus twins now realized that the Master’s life was moving swiftly toward its final culmination.
ch43.b018: About seven o’clock on Tuesday morning Jesus met the apostles, the women’s corps, and some two dozen leading disciples at Simon’s house. He said farewell to Lazarus, giving him the instruction that soon led him to flee to Philadelphia, said good-bye to the aged Simon, and gave his parting advice to the women. Then he greeted each of the twelve in turn. To Peter he said: “⟦Q 174:0.2⟧Put not your trust in the arm of flesh nor in weapons of steel. Establish yourself on the spiritual foundations of the eternal rocks.⟦/Q⟧” To John: “⟦Q 174:0.2⟧Be gentle; love even your enemies; be tolerant. And remember that I have trusted you with many things.⟦/Q⟧” To Thomas: “⟦Q 174:0.2⟧No matter how difficult it may be, just now you must walk by faith and not by sight.⟦/Q⟧” And to Judas Iscariot: “⟦Q 174:0.2⟧Judas, I have loved you and have prayed that you would love your brethren. Be not weary in well doing; and I would warn you to beware the slippery paths of flattery and the poison darts of ridicule.⟦/Q⟧”
ch43.b019: He set off for Jerusalem with Andrew, Peter, James, and John, while the others went to make ready the camp near Gethsemane. Halfway down the slope of Olivet he paused with the four for more than an hour, and Peter laid before him a question he and James had long disputed: Does the Father forgive us even before we ask, or must repentance and confession come first? Jesus answered by speaking of the understanding sympathy of a wise parent for an immature and sometimes erring child. “When a wise man understands the inner impulses of his fellows, he will love them. And when you love your brother, you have already forgiven him. … The child … must frequently feel a sense of guilty separation from a father’s full approval, but the true father is never conscious of any such separation. Sin is an experience of creature consciousness; it is not a part of God’s consciousness.”
ch43.b021: Jesus had spoken only a few words in the temple court when a group of younger students from the academies, rehearsed for the purpose and accompanied by Herodians, came forward with flattering words and a question: “⟦Q 174:2.2⟧Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar? Shall we give or shall we not give?⟦/Q⟧” If he said no, they would charge him with sedition before Pilate; if he said yes, he would wound the national pride of the crowd. “⟦Q 174:2.2⟧Why do you thus come to tempt me? Show me the tribute money, and I will answer you.⟦/Q⟧” When they handed him a denarius, he asked, “⟦Q 174:2.2⟧Whose image and superscription does this coin bear?⟦/Q⟧” They answered, “Caesar’s.” Then Jesus said, “⟦Q 174:2.2⟧Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and render to God the things that are God’s.⟦/Q⟧” Even the youths who had tried to trap him marveled at the wisdom of his answer.
ch43.b022: Next came a company of crafty Sadducees with the tale of a woman who had been married in turn to seven brothers, each dying childless: whose wife would she be in the resurrection? Jesus told them they knew neither the Scriptures nor the living power of God; those who attain the worlds to come neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of heaven. Moses himself had heard the Father say at the burning bush, “⟦Q 174:3.2⟧I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 174:3.2⟧And so, along with Moses, do I declare that my Father is not the God of the dead but of the living.⟦/Q⟧” Then a lawyer among the Pharisees asked which was the greatest commandment. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 174:4.2⟧‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, with all your mind and with all your strength.’ This is the first and great commandment. And the second commandment is like this first; … ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’⟦/Q⟧” When the lawyer openly commended the answer, Jesus said, “⟦Q 174:4.3⟧My friend, I perceive that you are not far from the kingdom of God.⟦/Q⟧” That very night the man went out to the camp near Gethsemane and was baptized. After this no one dared ask Jesus another question in public.
ch43.b023: As noon drew near, Jesus asked a question of his own: “⟦Q 174:4.6⟧What do you think of the Deliverer? That is, whose son is he?⟦/Q⟧” One of the scribes answered, “⟦Q 174:4.6⟧The Messiah is the son of David.⟦/Q⟧” Then how, Jesus asked, could David, speaking in the spirit, call him Lord in the Psalm, “⟦Q 174:4.6⟧The Lord said to my lord, sit on my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet⟦/Q⟧”? “⟦Q 174:4.6⟧If David calls him Lord, how then can he be his son?⟦/Q⟧” The rulers made no reply. Earlier the Pharisees had enjoyed the silencing of the Sadducees; now the Sadducees enjoyed the failure of the Pharisees. But that rivalry was only momentary. They soon forgot their old differences in the united effort to stop him.
ch43.b025: About noon, while Philip was buying supplies for the new camp, he was approached by a group of believing Greeks from Alexandria, Athens, and Rome, who said, “⟦Q 174:5.1⟧we come to you, Sir, with the request to see Jesus, your Master.⟦/Q⟧” Philip, perplexed, hurried to the house of Joseph to fetch Andrew, and the two of them brought the Greeks to the luncheon where Jesus sat with his apostles and leading disciples, Jews and gentiles in about equal numbers. Jesus spoke to them of the end of one dispensation and the beginning of another. “⟦Q 174:5.8⟧You well know that, except a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it abides alone; but if it dies in good soil, it springs up again to life and bears much fruit.⟦/Q⟧” Then he confessed that his soul was troubled. “⟦Q 174:5.9⟧Shall I say, Father save me from this awful hour? No! For this very purpose have I come into the world and even to this hour. Rather will I say, and pray that you will join me: Father, glorify your name; your will be done.⟦/Q⟧”
ch43.b026: When he had said this, the Personalized Adjuster of his indwelling during prebaptismal times appeared before him and spoke: “⟦Q 174:5.10⟧I have glorified my name in your bestowals many times, and I will glorify it once more.⟦/Q⟧” Those in the room heard no voice, but they saw the Master pause while a message came to him from some superhuman source, and they said to one another, “⟦Q 174:5.11⟧An angel has spoken to him.⟦/Q⟧” Then Jesus told them that he would go back with them to the temple and speak his farewell words to the rulers of Israel. They followed him through the narrow streets in silence.
ch43.b027: The Last Discourse in the Temple
ch43.b028: Shortly after two o’clock that Tuesday afternoon, accompanied by eleven apostles, Joseph of Arimathea, the thirty Greeks, and other disciples, Jesus began his last address in the temple courts. The money-changers had not dared to come back, and the court was quiet. He began with mercy. Even now, he said, his Father would receive these blinded teachers and hypocritical leaders if they would turn to him. “⟦Q 175:1.3⟧Even now it is not too late for this people to receive the word of heaven and to welcome the Son of Man.⟦/Q⟧” He bade his hearers co-operate with the scribes and Pharisees, who still sat in Moses’ seat, in everything related to the peace of Israel, but not to pattern after their works. “⟦Q 175:1.8⟧Remember, this is the sin of these rulers: They say that which is good, but they do it not.⟦/Q⟧” They bound heavy burdens on men’s shoulders and would not lift one finger to help carry them.
ch43.b029: Then the tone changed. “⟦Q 175:1.12⟧Woe upon you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!⟦/Q⟧” One indictment followed another: against those who shut the doors of the kingdom, who tithed mint, anise, and cumin but disregarded “⟦Q 175:1.17⟧the weightier matters of the law—faith, mercy, and judgment,⟦/Q⟧” who cleansed the outside of the cup and the platter while within remained the filth of extortion, who were like whited sepulchres, beautiful outside and full of dead men’s bones within. Yet at the end he held out his hand once more. “⟦Q 175:1.22,175:1.23,175:1.24⟧But even now I offer you in my Father’s name mercy and forgiveness. … O Jerusalem and the children of Abraham, you who have stoned the prophets and killed the teachers that were sent to you, even now would I gather your children together as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings, but you will not! … Behold, I now go forth with my children, and your house is left to you desolate!⟦/Q⟧” And he beckoned his followers to leave the temple.
ch43.b030: Judas did not hear the first, merciful half of that address. He was still at lunch with certain Sadducean relatives and friends, discussing the most fitting way to dissociate himself from Jesus. He returned in time for the denunciation, and it was while he listened to it that he finally and fully made up his mind to forsake the gospel movement. At eight o’clock that evening the Sanhedrin met, and just before midnight on Tuesday, April 4, A.D. 30, it officially and unanimously voted the death sentence upon both Jesus and Lazarus. That was its answer to the last offer of heavenly mercy ever extended to the Jewish nation as such. Yet the rejection of Jesus by the leaders of that nation in no way affects the standing of any individual Jew before God. Jesus himself was a Jew by birth, and so were the first martyrs of the gospel. The Father and his Creator Son have never ceased to love the Jews.
